scenario_text: Determine the effective contact rate used by an epidemic-control program that activates when measured prevalence reaches a specified trigger. Below the trigger, contacts remain at their baseline level; at or above it, a fixed fraction of contacts is suppressed. Prevalence, the uncontrolled contact rate, the trigger, and intervention strength are independently sampled policy conditions. The target is the immediate controlled contact rate, without modeling delayed behavioral adjustment.

response_change.parent_relation: For fixed c0 and p_trigger, c_eff is piecewise constant in p: equal to c0 below threshold and c0*(1-rho) at and above threshold, so once active the suppression strength does not vary with how far prevalence exceeds the trigger.
response_change.child_relation: Retain trigger activation at p_trigger, but replace constant active-phase suppression with prevalence-dependent suppression that strengthens smoothly as p rises further above the trigger, approaching a maximum reduction at high prevalence.
response_change.observable_effect: Holding c0, p_trigger, and the new active-phase shape fixed, two above-threshold prevalences produce different c_eff values in the child, whereas the parent predicts the same flat plateau for both.

evolution_plan.gap_statement: The current model assumes all above-threshold situations induce the same proportional contact reduction, ignoring that epidemic-control intensity and compliance often strengthen as measured prevalence rises further beyond the activation threshold.
evolution_plan.baseline_assumption: Compliance is constant whenever the intervention is active.
evolution_plan.scientific_mechanism: Within the active intervention regime, risk perception, enforcement, or policy tightening can make the suppressed contact fraction increase with prevalence excess above the trigger rather than remaining fixed.
evolution_plan.rationale: The parent target mapping has a single active-regime gain: vary p while holding c0, p_trigger, and rho fixed, and all p values below p_trigger map to c0 while all p values at or above p_trigger map to one constant plateau c0*(1-rho). A realistic refinement is to keep the same trigger but relax the idealization of constant active compliance, so the above-threshold branch acquires nonzero slope with respect to p and possibly saturates toward a maximum suppression. The distinguishing condition is to compare two admissible above-threshold prevalences, one just above p_trigger and one substantially larger, with the same c0, p_trigger, and intervention-strength setting. The child predicts lower c_eff at the larger prevalence, while the parent with any single shared parameter set must give identical c_eff for both because its active branch is flat. This changes the scored target mapping itself, not merely an auxiliary trajectory. The contrast is scientifically admissible when prevalence spans the active regime; if all observed p are either below threshold or confined to a narrow band immediately above it, the refinement may be weakly identifiable, and that limitation should be acknowledged.

derivation_notes: The parent used a single active-regime excess scale proportional only to p_trigger. Here the post-trigger suppression growth is re-scaled by p_trigger + p_trigger**2, so the threshold gate remains the same but the exponential tightening competes with a trigger-level-dependent administrative distance above threshold before strong suppression accumulates.
change_summary: I relaxed the assumption that all trigger settings share one universal post-trigger curvature when expressed versus relative excess prevalence. The successor keeps the same activation gate but makes the approach to maximal suppression depend on the trigger level itself, changing the target mapping across policies with different p_trigger.

assumption_audit.released_assumption: A single normalized prevalence-excess scale ((p-p_trigger)/p_trigger) fully determines active-regime suppression curvature for all trigger settings.
assumption_audit.mechanism: Administrative response and behavioral escalation can depend on both trigger crossing and the absolute distance above the trigger, so the depth of suppression need not rise with the same curvature for all trigger levels.
assumption_audit.parent_reduction: The parent is recovered when the threshold-dependent active-regime rescaling reduces back to p_trigger, i.e. when the extra trigger dependence in the suppression-growth scale is removed.

response_change.parent_relation: For fixed c0, p_trigger, and rho, the active-regime suppression grows monotonically with prevalence excess through a single saturation shape set entirely by the normalized excess (p-p_trigger)/p_trigger, so the post-trigger contact-rate decline has one shared curvature pattern across thresholds.
response_change.child_relation: Keep the same trigger-centered activation but replace the normalized excess scale with a threshold-dependent normalization so that the steepness and saturation distance above threshold depend on the trigger level itself; low-trigger policies can tighten more abruptly after crossing than high-trigger policies, or vice versa, even at the same normalized excess.
response_change.observable_effect: Holding c0 and rho fixed, compare two policies with different p_trigger. As p rises above each trigger, the parent predicts the same suppression trajectory when plotted against (p-p_trigger)/p_trigger, whereas the child predicts different post-trigger curvature or approach-to-saturation across those trigger values.

evolution_contract.scientific_mechanism: Administrative response and behavioral escalation often depend on both crossing the trigger and how far prevalence exceeds it in absolute terms, making low-threshold and high-threshold policies differ in how quickly suppression deepens after activation.
evolution_contract.difficulty_rationale: This is harder than a coefficient correction because the active suppression process now competes against a trigger-dependent saturation distance, creating different post-trigger curvature across p_trigger values rather than one universal profile that can be shifted or rescaled by refitting rho alone.

evolution_contract.assumption_after: After activation, suppression growth depends on a threshold-dependent excess scale, so trigger level modifies the active-regime curvature and saturation distance.

The parent gives the same suppression-versus-relative-excess curve because all active-regime dependence is through (p-p_trigger)/p_trigger, but the child gives distinct bends because the exponential deepening now depends separately on p_trigger through the threshold-dependent denominator.
